If you can think of any, let me know. Doesn't matter what country, year or even genre. Just using *No Country for Old Men* as a framing point.

## 2. [spoiler] Live-action action films where the villain survives and wins. The hero fails. Not a part one movie like Infinity War or a set series like Harry Potter. Just a straight up, the hero failed, movie’s over. Villain won. Not horror or thriller. Straight action movie.

**Score:** 44
**Body:** I’m curious because I’ve never seen a live-action action film where this happened. I’ve seen anti-hero stuff or seen it in horror movies or thrillers (Sinister, Seven, etc.). Although Seven he didn’t survive, obviously, but that was by design. I’ve seen it in dramas (No Country for Old Men).

I’m sure it exists, but I cannot recall an action film that’s just a straight up hero failed that’s a stand alone film. It’s ok if it’s part of a series just not part of a pre-set thing like Infinity War and Endgame or Harry Potter where the story lines connect. If it’s a sequel that doesn’t fully continue the story of the last one (e.g. Spider-Man 2, then it would be fine). Like imagine if in Spider-Man 2, Doc Oc beat Peter Parker and his plan fully worked, and he survived. That’s what I’m looking for. Not a story just like that, but a story that works that way. Another example would be if in The Dark Knight, The Joker got away, and Batman didn’t save the family from Harvey Dent. Just a full on, I win, you lose.

Edit: Please remember, straight action film with a clear hero who fails. Villain wins.

I knew I'd probably like it cuz it be camp but this literally exceeded my expectations so much.

Derek Cho  ( Steven Yeun) A tired but proud of his job guy is working an  exhausting  job at a consulting firm until" the Siren " Kara Powell gets him fired for something he didn't do. While he is about to leave with his stuff in a box. The whole building is shut down due to a virus called the red eye leading people to act against their morals. 

Melanie Cross (Samara weaving) is a  Client of the firm who tries to prevent herself from losing her house by  pretending to be her lawyer in hopes to get somebody to give her more time to pay her loan but it is quickly realized that she's not and she is escorted away from the premises but before they can take her outside the building is shut down due to a virus called the red eye. 

These two must work together to get what they want...... Revenge. 

(I hope This was a good synopsis. I'm not really great at writing them)



Where I watched : Tubi

Genre: Horror comedy

Rating: 10/10

My likes about this movie:

\- This movie is hilarious (literally not one bad joke in this movie)

\- The chemistry and dynamic between Steven and Samaras characters is so good and they are so cute

\- I like the small details they put into some of the characters (there's a character nicknamed The reaper that has a cane and the cane is very closely shaped to a scythe. It looks really cool)

\- The premise is creative and hilarious

\- They pulled off the sad parts of this movie very well surprisingly

\- This movie was very well balanced between comedy, horror, intensity and sadness (One of the deaths made me so sad)

\- Everybody's acting was very good

\- I loved this new version of a "zombie" it was really cool to see.

\- The fight scenes were really good. They felt realistic, they were very well coordinated.

\- This movie made me realize how much I need Steven Yeun in a villain roll (If he's in any movies as a villain please let me know cuz I want to see them )

And Samara was great too ( if there's any movies with her as a villain let me know because I'd want to watch that too)

My Gripes about this movie:

N/A(I literally had none not even if I try to nitpick or anything ,this movie was that good)

 Absolutely! This was such a fun movie that I feel I could watch over and over again and never get tired of, I love this movie!

## 5. Digger is one of the most ambitious Hollywood swings in recent memory. Wrote my thoughts on it

**Score:** 17
**Body:** I have finally put my hat in the Digger discourse. Dig dig dig. I'm so glad Tom Cruise has joined forces with another auteur in his catalog. The discourse surrounding Digger has heavily centered on the massive $150–180 million budget, and how big of a creative and financial risk this has been for everybody involved. Along, with critics lambasting it for the lack of "humor" and self-indulgent tendencies both stylistically and politically. It certainly has a lot to say about current politics, overconsumption, power, and environmental catastrophe. Digger has safely divided fans and critics alike.

Having seen it, I lean FOR Digger. I adored it. I was especially interested in how the film uses its absurdist humor and Cruise’s larger-than-life performance to explore a world that feels increasingly farcical. It lets out all the current frustrations about where we are going and sums it up in an entertaining, loud fashion. I don't know how else one can encapsulate what we're all feeling. What stuck with me most, though, was how it illustrates the complicated relationship with creating art, especially political art, when you don't have power to change the things you're criticizing. The feeling of powerlessness that comes with watching the world fall apart.

I wrote a review exploring why I think the film’s ambition and messiness are part of what make it so interesting.

I’d genuinely love to hear what other people think. Does Digger earn its swings, or does its ambition get the better of it? And what do you think the film says about the place of original, auteur-driven movies in Hollywood today? I'm sure you all have thoughts LOL.

**My extended thoughts:** [Digger Review: Satirizing a Satirical World](https://substack.com/@awhfilms/note/p-219669922?utm_source=notes-share-action&r=38m95e)

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Throwing my hat in the Digger Discourse. The absurdity of making art about a world you cannot change.

**Score:** 74
**Body:** I've finally put my hat into the Digger discourse, and I have a lot of thoughts. The most interesting idea the film presents, to me, is the tension between political art as a form of protest and the uncomfortable reality that making art about a crisis doesn't necessarily do anything to stop it.

Digger has been a fascinatingly divisive film. Much of the discourse lies in the film's $150–180 million budget and its aggressively political satire. I don't personally get the hate coming from critical circles, especially the daggers for Iñarritu personally. I can understand why the film appears self-indulgent or pretentious, but to me, a film is only that when it gives nothing back to the audience. But, I found Digger to be really really funny. And super entertaining. Once the infamous twist is revealed I still found it terribly fascinating. It's a film that makes very little effort to temper its ambitions or make itself palatable. Personally, I loved it.

What I found most compelling was how Iñárritu uses absurdist comedy to approach a world that already feels absurd. The film's political targets are hardly subtle: corporate power, environmental catastrophe, political opportunism, overconsumption, and the various hypocrisies that allow these systems to persist. But I thought the humor worked best when it emerged naturally from the characters and the situations rather than feeling like a punchline engineered to make sure the audience understood the joke.

But the element I keep returning to is the film's relationship with art itself. What does it mean to create political art when the problems you're criticizing seem too entrenched to change? What does satire accomplish when audiences can laugh at the absurdity of the world, but then choose to engage with the world the exact way corporate powers and politicians want you to behave. 

I found the film's treatment of these questions more complicated than either a straightforward celebration of satire or a nihilistic dismissal of its power. There's a kind of ambivalence at work here. The film recognizes how easily political outrage becomes entertainment, but it also seems to believe there's something valuable in the creative act itself. Art may not give us the power to change the world, but perhaps it can give us a temporary way to confront the people and systems that make us feel powerless.

I'm curious how others here interpreted the film, particularly its relationship with political satire and artistic expression. Does Digger meaningfully interrogate the limits of political art? Can a film acknowledge the limitations of satire while still functioning as a great satire?

I wrote my extended thoughts in a Substack review if anyone is interested: 

[Digger Review: Satirizing a Satirical World](https://abhinavyerramreddy.substack.com/p/digger-review-satirizing-a-satirical?r=38m95e&utm_campaign=post-expanded-share&utm_medium=post%20viewer)

### Top 3 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. In my opinion, this film has nothing to do with climate change, Trump, politics, religion, oil, war, acting, film, cinema none of it. It’s much bigger than that.

Digger's speech in Europe is directed at you, me, us. We don't want it to stop. We pay for it to go on. We vote with our choices. And ultimately, we’d all rather be entertained to death than face real life for even one moment.

McCarthy's Judge in Blood Meridian said *war is god.* Innaritu said nope, hold my beer, *entertainment is.*
  - >Digger's speech in Europe is directed at you, me, us. We don't want it to stop. We pay for it to go on. We vote with our choices. And ultimately, we’d all rather be entertained to death than face real life for even one moment.

This is very much a problem with a lot of movies of this sort. I've spoken before about the idea of first/second/third cinema, and seeing more and more of these big budget movies that support the idea of the purpose of second cinema, while having budgets typically associated with what would be considered first cinema, seems to only support the accuracy of that view. I've also been playing around with an idea in my head for awhile of "liberal nihilism"-basically movies (such as this) that show the terrible state of the world in some way and may even point at the causes, but essentially throw up their hands at the end and say "ehh, nothing to be done just the way that things are, there's nothing really better". The reason being, that any movie that genuinely points at society's ills and also the systemic changes needed to address them isn't going to get Tom Cruise to star and have a $150 million budget. 

None of this is saying your read is incorrect, or that it's bad. If anything I think it's a very interesting way of seeing the movie and likely has a good amount of truth. It does point to Iñárritu's extremely liberal framing of things though (and why someone is able to get funding for a movie that superficially challenges a lot of powerful figures/structures in society)-it takes systemic issues and assigns blame to individuals. Worse, it assigns blame to the most powerless individuals in the situation. It ignores entirely the efforts from the very forces being criticized in the movie to deliberately and intentionally mislead, propagandize, browbeat, bribe, and otherwise destroy the will of people to resist what is happening. It's like how financial literacy types try to sell the idea that the only reason anyone is poor is because they haven't done enough investing and started their own LLC, ignoring the fact that for many people they don't have the money to invest in the first place. 

I know that was a bit long-winded, but I've been finding myself more and more frustrated with these movies that seem to flirt with critiquing power structures yet in the end lead people away from conclusions that would lead them to be able to work against them (OBAA, Eddington, Triangle of Sadness, I Love Boosters, Bugonia, etc etc). And while I obviously don't expect nor need to have movies with perfect politics, or even match mine (hell, I still recommend things like Bone Tomahawk to people), it is I find more obnoxious when they seem to handwave in that direction to only zag at the last moment.

    - We are the villain in this movie, it's no wonder people hate it.🙃
      - No one likes a mirror held up to themselves 
2. I shouldn’t be commenting cause I haven’t seen the film but I do think it’s peculiar anyone thinks the function of art is to change the world. It’s simply to interface with the world.
  - > “During the Vietnam War… every respectable artist in this country was against the war. It was like a laser beam. We were all aimed in the same direction.
>

— Kurt Vonnegut

## 2. Digger is a meta-commentary on the limits of fiction

**Score:** 32
**Body:** I came away from Digger feeling like I watched a different movie than most critics or viewers.

>!Kenny Rockwell nearly directly states that the play doesn’t matter in the grand scheme of things, that it is catharsis for the audience who hate his uncle. And everyone is complicit with his vision, especially Martson who is happy to use Rockwell’s spy network / intel company to find his daughter.!<

>!The last scene blew me away. All these well off New Yorkers are putting on their fancy air filtration masks to leave the theater and it’s a fasicst hellscape out there. I thought Iñárritu was really challenging the audience to ask what it would take to stop a man like Digger and the system he represents rather than getting fictional revenge. I think if’s also a dig at Hollywood pretension about films that “matter” when it comes to truly massive problems like climate change. This all struck me as less subtle than Don’t Look Up, which used an asteroid metaphor whole Digger was so explicit about climate change while making the peril immediate with the glaciers breaking off.!<

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. This is what I took from the film as well. He's of the ruling class and he bought the rights to the play so that people can go and see it and think "yes, someone else is making important art that raises awareness of this issue, so I don't need to do anything else". And that's precisely what we the audience are doing too

I haven't read any reviews but the limits of art as activism is precisely the message I got. The system is very good at absorbing and deradicalising its opposition
  - I ageee with this and OP, the film reminded me of Michael Haneke and his philosophy regarding filmmaking ("we are all complicit")
2. Yeah this was the main point that I came away with that there is only so much political art can accomplish. But I don't agree with people saying that this makes the film end on a dour or overly hopeless note. I think as you said it speaks to the limit of art. It can't change the situation dramatically and there's something farcical about staging a massive artistic production that costs millions of dollars to critique the people endlessly hoarding millions of dollars and not contributing to the people. Digger rightfully pokes fun at and exposes the recent trend of "preachy" films and films "of our times". But, it's not a premise that promotes inaction, but celebrates the momentary catharsis where art gives power back to the people they're never set up to have.
3. I think it's mostly an observational film that is willing to acknowledge the reality and consequences of climate change without trying to pretend we can still do much about it. Our government isn't competent enough, our oligarchs aren't willing to give up profits, and our populace isn't organized or motivated enough to overthrow either group. I think a lot of people are sick of pretending that the future isn't a dystopian hellscape or that this is somehow hard to see coming. Digger blows off the idea that climate change isn't real or isn't caused by emissions, it blows off the idea that we're going to do anything about it, and a lot of people who enjoy the film are happy to see a piece of art that simply acknowledges what should be obvious to anyone looking beyond the turmoil of the current administration.
  - This. I think it was one of the most hopeless films I’ve ever seen, and that was refreshing in a sense. Succession was the same way to me. Just a totally pessimistic, yet clear eyed view of things. 
    - What do you take from the whole “hope (daughter’s name) is alive” bit at the end? Meant to be interpreted literally? Or was it a sort of meta fake out - this info comes from digger’s nephew who owns a very dystopian global security company, given to make the main actor in his play (and us) feel good, right before the hellscape reveal. 
  - Another key scene is Digger and the scientist both thinking they are telling “the truth” and how that’s ultimately useful to Digger.
    - Part of Digger's thesis is just that, truth doesn't matter anymore. The facts are irrelevant, if they even exist. It's all about the story being told.
4. Ive seen people make this point like 60 times and what I just don't get is what's interesting about it? Yea a play isn't gonna solve a crisis caused by much bigger powers how is that an interesting point in any way and how it is worth yelling at me at the top of its lungs for 2+ hours 
  - I don't think the point is "art can't fix it." It's that there are no "bigger powers" separate from us. Your 401k is in oil. Your lights run on the grid. We ALL built this trap.

The future audience blames one cartoon oil guy, cries, cheers, then puts on gas masks and goes about their day in flooded streets. The catharsis is how they get off the hook.

If it didn't land for you, fair enough. But "a crisis caused by much bigger powers" is pretty much exactly what the movie is making fun of.

## 3. Thoughts on how the conditions surrounding the viewing of a film affects the experience of watching it

**Score:** 32
**Body:** Recently, I discovered this arthouse-adjacent theater in my city, which is like 30 minutes by foot. So, yesterday, I went there for the first time for a screening of Everybody Knows (2018) dir. Asghar Farhadi. Now, while the screen and the seating were actually kinda subpar compared to my local chain theater, the vibes were - and I don't say this lightly - FUCKING IMMACULATE.

The theater itself is situated in an old restored church. The seating is surrounded on both sides by greek-style nude statues, and on the walls beyond those statues, hanged large colorful murals. Above the statues, between the murals, were 6 HUGE wall-mounted fans, 3 on each side, to ensure proper air circulation — and while they were not quiet, they were clearly intentionally designed and spaced in such a way that their noise would blend in with the background. A minute after they had been turned on, I had already forgotten they were even there. All of that gave this place some type of *je ne sais quoi* that made just being there vaguely enjoyable.

The film started, and I discovered another immense joy that I hadn't considered: the audience. They were diverse of age; some young, some old, one of them even *concerningly* old, but they all had one thing in common — they had come to this niche arthouse theater that's actually in a restored church, to watch a screening of a 2018 film with 60k views on letterboxd. They were all - at least to some extent - cinephiles. And they knew to follow theater etiquette.

The theater was packed full, but it was so silent. No one photographed the title screen and blinded the audience with their flash. Heck, there wasn't a phone to be found in sight. Very few of them had popcorn or any snacks, and those who did, knew not to munch loudly. No one whispered to their friends. When one person had to leave, they did so very discretely. And, get this, they didn't do an intermission during this 2 hour and 15 minutes film (even a less than 90 minute film will typically have an intermission here, I know, its awful).

The film gripped me hard in a way films rarely and I enjoyed it thoroughly from beginning to end. Its the kind of gripping where you forget that your bladder is full. When the credits rolled and the light came on, I actually looked around and had to gather where I was for like 3 seconds — which is an awesome feeling that I hadn't felt literally since I was a child. So, having just had this really amazing experience, I naturally walked out of the theater, hungry as all hell, bladder full, and had a mini-existential crisis during the 30 minute walk home.

Was it really the film that I enjoyed, or the theater? Or, to put it another way, even if the film is good, just how much did this experience elevate it? One of the things I enjoyed most about the film is the sound design — would my kinda shitty flatscreen that I watch most films on have done it justice? How many films have I watched were hindered by the fact that I can't afford a better TV or a better sound system?

Even beyond that my flat screen, my local chain theater has different sizes of halls, some are better, some worse. One of them has an absolutely humongous screen (not IMAX, just really big screen) and amazing sound. Another has really low sound/speakers. Recently, I watched Digger on that really big screen in an empty hall, and it became my third fave film of the year. But it was only there for 2 days, before it was moved to a shittier screen (no one was watching it). Would it have been my third fave of the year if I had gotten around to seeing it 2 days later?

And even beyond just me, how does that affect discussions surrounding art, and in particular, film? Have the people that have seen Zone of Interest at home really experienced the same film as those that saw it in a theater? What about Oppenheimer? What about The Odyssey, and how the people who will see it at home will have it at a completely different aspect ratio than standard or IMAX? People will always have different personal experiences with a film, but sometimes I wonder—

At last, I had arrived to my apartment. I rush to the bathroom and have a really humongous piss.

Sometimes I wonder, how much of film discussion is people having different experiences to the *same stimulus* due to personal taste versus people having different experiences due to coming in contact with *fundamentally different stimuli*.

## 4. Two contrasting romances in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000).

**Score:** 29
**Body:** Just got done watching this great film. There is a lot that can be said about the film, but for now, I will stick to the two contrasting love stories in the film, and how each is well realized.

Firstly, there is the silent, respectful and deep romance shared between Master Li Mu Bai and Michelle Yeoh's Yu Shu Lien. There is a sense of honor associated with it, along with calmness, quiet longing and something even spiritual that defines it. There is nothing explicit or physical about this relationship, but the confession of love in the end by Master Li Mu Bai hits hard and deep. This romance we can say is like water; calm, cool but deep. And the resolution of their relationship is also likewise.

On the other hand is the fiery romance between Jen Yu and Dark Cloud. That is what can happen when young people can fall in love. It's passionate, intense, physical and defined by grand gestures. And the conclusion of this particular relationship is also made through a dramatic act by Jen Yu (which by the way I am still wondering why she jumped to her death. Guilt perhaps?).

I did not know that a wuxia film with some of the best fight choreography put to a film would involve two touching and well developed romance stories. Great film by Ang Lee.
